guard: the declaration beside the reaper is what the compiler emits from the reaper, so the two cannot describe different modules
why: reap-smoke-brokers.mjs stays plain JavaScript because it runs on the CI runner before any workspace build, so its .ts consumers need a declaration beside it. Two hand written guards over a hand written declaration each passed GREEN over real drift, because each was an enumeration of the shapes its author thought of. The declaration is now emitted from the module and compared byte for byte, so there is no shape to recognise. Mutations 1 through 9 are each a shape that beat one of those guards, or the mirror of one, and every one of those must move the SAME cell: that is the property, that the kind of change does not matter. Row 10 is deliberately not one of them and moves a different cell on purpose: it turns the module's type checking OFF, which the first nine all silently depend on, and it is named by the guard that reads the property rather than the one that compares bytes. The completion marker is the suite's own final banner, which it prints on either outcome, so a run that dies before reaching the cell grades INCONCLUSIVE rather than passing as a kill.

mutations.name: an export is RENAMED in the module and the declaration does not follow
mutations.expectRed: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.cell: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module

mutations.name: an export is ADDED to the module and the declaration does not follow
mutations.replace:
export const SMOKE_BROKER_PREFIX = "cotal-smoke-broker-";
export const REAPER_VERSION = 2;
mutations.expectRed: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.cell: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.note: The MIRROR of the rename. A guard that only checks declared-implies-present calls an undeclared export fine, and an undeclared export is what an untyped consumer then reads with no type at all.

mutations.name: a REQUIRED parameter is added AFTER a defaulted one, so Function.length does not move
mutations.replace: export function reportReaped(label, result, onDone = () => {}, finalRequired) {
mutations.expectRed: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.cell: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.note: The exact input that beat the previous guard, and the reason arity is no longer compared at all. Function.length is the count of parameters BEFORE THE FIRST DEFAULT, not the count of parameters that are required: this mutant carries four parameters and reports length 2, so a guard comparing it against a declaration that says two printed agreement about a signature that had changed underneath it. An earlier version of this note said the real call site, shard.mjs reportReaped(cmd, after), threw TypeError at runtime. A security review refuted that and it is corrected here: JavaScript enforces no required parameter, so that call binds finalRequired to undefined and returns (measured on the planted mutant: functionLength=2, two-argument-call=returned). There is no runtime input that makes a JavaScript arity mutant fatal, so this row does not promise one. What kills it is the module's own JSDoc under // @ts-check: gen:reaper-dts exits 1 with Parameter 'finalRequired' implicitly has an 'any' type, before any declaration is emitted to compare. Nothing here counts parameters, so there is nothing to count wrongly.

mutations.name: an alias RE-EXPORT is added to the module and the declaration does not follow
mutations.replace:
export const SMOKE_BROKER_PREFIX = "cotal-smoke-broker-";
export { SMOKE_BROKER_PREFIX as PREFIX_ALIAS };
mutations.expectRed: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.cell: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.note: One of three forms that landed in NEITHER side of the previous guard's comparison: the alias is not a variable statement so the parse missed it, and it is a declaration-only name so the module key set missed it too. Both directions agreed by being equally blind, which is the worst way for a comparison to pass.

mutations.cell: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module

mutations.name: a NAMESPACE MERGE is added to an exported function and the declaration does not follow
mutations.find:
for (const { pid, args } of result.reaped) console.log(`  [reaper]   killed pid ${pid}: ${args.slice(0, 120)}`);
}
mutations.expectRed: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.cell: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.note: The third form. A merged member reads as declared and resolves to undefined at runtime, which is the failure a declaration is supposed to prevent. The expando now sits BELOW the function it merges into, and where it sits is the whole point: anchored on the signature line, the inserted statement landed between the JSDoc block and the declaration, the JSDoc re-attached to the expando, the function lost its @param types, and the generator threw an implicit-any BEFORE the emitted bytes were ever compared. The cell went red, but on @ts-check catching a detached comment, which mutation 7 already covers. It was a mislabeled duplicate that never reached the property its name claims. Anchored on the last line of the body plus the closing brace, the JSDoc stays attached, the emit gains `export namespace reportReaped { let version: string; }`, and the cell reds on the byte comparison, naming the first differing byte. The find is still code only, because a find that spans a comment is disarmed by anyone tidying the comment and smoke:mutation-fixtures refuses one.

mutations.name: a field's TYPE drifts in the module while its name stays
mutations.expectRed: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.cell: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.note: Neither previous guard compared a single type, so a pid that became a string was agreement: names matched, arity matched, the report's field set matched. This one is killed by the module's own JSDoc under // @ts-check rather than by the bytes, and the cell reports the compiler's message instead of a diff, because the generator refuses to emit a declaration it could not typecheck.

mutations.name: the generated declaration is hand edited and the module does not follow
mutations.find: export function reportReaped(label: string, result: ReapReport): void;
mutations.replace: export function reportReaped(label: string, result: ReapReport, onDone: () => void): void;
mutations.expectRed: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.cell: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.note: The mirror direction. The generated file carries a do-not-edit banner, and this is what makes that banner enforceable rather than advisory. What the edit buys is a declaration promising a parameter the module does not have: a `.ts` consumer writing reportReaped(cmd, after, done) compiles, and `done` is then silently dropped and never called. Nothing throws, exactly as nothing throws in the row above, so this row promises a silent wrong result and not a crash. The cell reads no shapes out of the declaration, so the hand edit is caught as bytes that are not what the compiler emits.

mutations.name: the module uses a library feature BEYOND the consumers' lib, which a looser generator would emit as any
mutations.replace:
export const SMOKE_BROKER_PREFIX = "cotal-smoke-broker-";
export const FUTURE_PAIR = Promise.withResolvers();
mutations.expectRed: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.cell: the committed declaration is what the compiler emits from the module
mutations.note: The generator's OWN configuration is a boundary, and an instrument does not verify its own boundary, so the boundary gets a mutant. An earlier version of this generator hand listed target ESNext while the consumers are checked at target ES2022 and lib ES2023. Under that pairing this exact line emitted PromiseWithResolvers<any>, the repository's skipLibCheck let a consumer swallow the unresolved type as any, and a consumer could then be compiled green against operations the runtime does not have: the declaration certified a lie and the suite stayed at 21 passed. The generator now reads the root tsconfig.json, the project that actually typechecks those consumers, so the same line fails loud instead: Property 'withResolvers' does not exist on type 'PromiseConstructor'. This mutation is what stops a future edit from restating the options and reopening it.

mutations.name: the module's type checking is turned OFF, which every row above silently depends on
mutations.expectRed: the module's JSDoc is really being checked: a deliberate type error in it stops the emit
mutations.cell: the module's JSDoc is really being checked: a deliberate type error in it stops the emit
mutations.note: Three rows above are killed by the module's JSDoc rather than by the emitted bytes, so they all rest on the module being checked, and until this row nothing mutated that. It could not: the check was asserted by reading `// @ts-check` off line 1, an anchor on it is prose, and smoke:mutation-fixtures refuses a find that spans a comment. The guard is now behavioural, so the anchor can be code. `// @ts-nocheck` above the import is still leading trivia and still disables the file, while `// @ts-check` stays on line 1 and the old read stayed GREEN through exactly this. Measured on this tree: the declaration cell stays GREEN here and only this cell reds, which is the point, since the drift rows are the ones this protects.

mutations.name: the RUNTIME drifts under a declaration that still reads as true
mutations.expectRed: and that same consumer RUNS against the module, so the declaration describes the code and not just its comments
mutations.cell: and that same consumer RUNS against the module, so the declaration describes the code and not just its comments
mutations.note: Every row above ties the declaration to the module's JSDoc, and a double cast is the one thing `// @ts-check` cannot see through, so a JSDoc that lies about its own implementation emits a declaration that lies too. A security review built exactly that (`@param {number} label` plus a cast back to string before a string-only use) and the suite stayed at 23 of 23. This row is the mirror: the declaration still promises a string and the code now demands a number of it, which no comparison of bytes or of comments can see. Only the executed consumer can, and it is the cell that reds.
